findings.matters: A lender assessing creditworthiness must see whether identified savings can address budget pressures. Savings declining while deficits grow signals worsening financial position and financial sustainability risk.

findings.matters: A finance director at West Devon or another council, and any lender, requires visibility of budget deficits to assess whether they can be closed and by what mechanism, as they affect financial sustainability and future borrowing capacity.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A: Integrated Performance Management Report: April – July 2026
findings.headline: Council approved insourcing of waste, street cleaning and toilet services as collection performance deteriorates
findings.detail: West Devon has approved bringing household waste, street cleaning and toilet services in-house from FCC Environment at contract end, with a project team established for delivery. Waste collection performance is simultaneously deteriorating: missed collections rose from 52 per 100,000 in April to 97 in July, exceeding the 80 per 100,000 national target, with absolute numbers rising from 92 to 179 missed collections. The insourcing is tracked as strategic risk SRR11, with one of five Waste theme actions reported as slightly off track and recycling officer recruitment flagged as a challenge.
findings.matters: Major operational change with significant financial and contractual implications; declining performance by current contractor during transition period suggests either service failure or underlying capacity issues that the insourcing business case must address

findings.matters: Significant structural change to a key council revenue source affects income planning across authorities facing similar reset impact.

findings.headline: Government funding reduced 7.5% (£0.276m) between 2025/26 and 2028/29 following Fair Funding Review

findings.matters: Demonstrates structural funding pressure on rural councils, relevant to how peer councils manage similar constraints.

findings.detail: In February 2026, the council forecast a budget gap over £500,000 for 2027/28. Through service reviews, income generation, and efficiency measures, the forecast gap has been reduced to £149,600. Services were asked to identify savings without impacting direct core service delivery.
findings.matters: Shows whether a council can execute savings plans in practice, not just identify them on paper.
findings.figures: Gap now £149,600 (1.4% of £10.857m net budget), down from £500,000+; savings identified £575,200

The Waste & Cleansing Options Review Reserve carries commitments for waste infrastructure improvements and transition mobilisation costs, projected to decline from £980k to £606k across the two-year period.

findings.detail: A contribution of £200k to the Financial Stability Reserve was approved during 2026/27 budget setting specifically to assist meeting a budget gap identified for 2027/28. The reserve begins at £474k and is fully depleted by end of 2027/28 after funding Council Plan commitments.
findings.matters: Anticipatory pre-funding of a specific future budget gap indicates the council has identified structural pressures for 2027/28 but is relying on reserves rather than addressing underlying cost or revenue issues.

findings.detail: The Business Rates Retention Reserve, designed to manage year-on-year volatility in business rates income, is funding recurring costs: £70k in 2026/27 and £200k in 2027/28 are earmarked to contribute to the base budget. Additionally, £1.25m is allocated from this reserve for Local Government Reorganisation costs in 2027/28, even though the council identifies that around £1m must be retained in the reserve for its volatility management function.
findings.matters: A volatility buffer being drawn for recurring budget costs suggests structural underfunding rather than temporary pressures; the £1.25m LGR commitment in the same year creates a peak funding need during a period of broader reserve depletion.

An amount of around £1m needs to be retained in the reserve to address the fluctuations in business rates income and business rates volatility. It is anticipated that £1.25m will need to be used for Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) in 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D – Reserves;
findings.headline: Total revenue reserves falling from £14.9m to £8.5m over two years, declining from 169% to 78% of net revenue budget
findings.detail: The council's total revenue reserves are projected to decline from £14.881m in March 2026 to £8.493m by March 2028. As a proportion of the annual budget, reserves shrink from 169% to 78%. Both earmarked and unearmarked reserves decline, with earmarked reserves planned to fall from £12.8m to £6.5m while the unearmarked reserve (general fund balance) remains static at £2.04m.
findings.matters: A reserve ratio falling from 169% to 78% of budget over two years indicates sustained drawdown of accumulated balances rather than rebuild, raising questions about the council's medium-term resilience to volatility or unexpected pressures.
findings.quote: Revenue Reserves 14,881,000 11,739,000 8,493,000; Reserves as a percentage of Net Revenue Budget 169% 119% 78%

findings.paper_title: Debt write offs
findings.headline: Housing Benefit overpayments written off fell 99.8% to £5.79 in Q1 2026/27, with £24k collected in the quarter
findings.detail: Housing Benefit overpayments written off fell from £2,819.96 in Q1 2025/26 to £5.79 in Q1 2026/27, due to reduced cases where overpayments are legally unrecoverable due to DWP or LA error. The council collected £24k in overpaid Housing Benefit during the quarter. A dedicated Housing Benefit Overpayments Recovery Officer appointed as a shared post with South Hams District Council is reported to have been instrumental in this improvement.
findings.matters: Housing Benefit recovery is a key income stream for the council. The dedicated officer role is delivering improvement in both collection and reduced write-offs, indicating effective operational management in the face of rising resident financial stress.
findings.figures: Q1 2025/26 write-offs: £2,819.96; Q1 2026/27 write-offs: £5.79; Q1 2026/27 collections: £24k
findings.quote: The decision to appoint a dedicated Housing Benefit Overpayments Recovery Officer (a shared post with South Hams District Council) has been instrumental in helping the Council maximise its collection performance.

findings.paper_title: Debt write offs
findings.headline: Council Tax collection rate of 98.13% in 2025/26 placed council 29th of 296 councils nationally, in top quartile
findings.detail: West Devon's Council Tax collection rate of 98.13% in 2025/26 exceeded the shire district average of 97.02% and placed the council in the top quartile nationally. This demonstrates strong underlying collection performance despite the rising write-offs.
findings.matters: Strong collection rates provide confidence in cash flow stability and suggest that rising write-offs are exceptions affecting a small proportion of debtors rather than signs of systemic collection weakness.
findings.figures: 98.13% collection rate; 29th of 296 councils nationally; shire district average 97.02%
findings.quote: The Council has above average collection rates for Council Tax having achieved an in-year collection rate of 98.13% in 2025/26. National collection rates were published on 25 June 2026 and this performance has placed the Council 29th of 296 Councils nationally and comfortably in the top quartile.

findings.paper_title: Debt write offs
findings.headline: Council Tax write-offs doubled to £34,815.11 in Q1 2026/27, driven by residents entering Debt Relief Orders and Individual Voluntary Arrangements
findings.detail: Debts approved for write-off by the Section 151 Officer increased from £17,349.54 in Q1 2025/26 to £34,815.11 in Q1 2026/27. Insolvency cases rose from 5 to 17. The paper attributes this to residents entering formal insolvency arrangements and notes that while 'many people are struggling with debt', they are 'seeking professional advice to deal with it', so the council may receive dividends as the arrangements progress.
findings.matters: The doubling of write-offs signals changing financial pressures on residents in the council's area. A finance director needs to understand whether this trend will continue and whether future bad debt provisions should adjust accordingly.
findings.quote: The amount of debt approved for write off by the Section 151 Officer under delegated powers has doubled when compared to the same quarter in 2025/26. There is a marked increase due to residents entering Debt Relief Orders and Individual Voluntary arrangements.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Capital Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: £14.9m investment property portfolio generates surplus rental income relied upon to support revenue budget sustainability
findings.detail: Council holds investment properties valued at £14.905m as at 31 March 2025. Investment Strategy explicitly requires tenant rental income to exceed PWLB debt-servicing costs, with surplus directed to revenue budget. Council maintains Maintenance, Management and Risk Mitigation Reserve at 15% of all rental income, with balance exceeding £890,000 as at 31 March 2026.
findings.matters: Revenue budget sustainability depends on sustained rental income from investment properties; disruption to tenancies, income streams, or market conditions directly impacts council's ability to service £25m debt and maintain service delivery
findings.figures: £14.9m investment portfolio value, 15% maintenance reserve requirement, reserve balance £890,000+
findings.quote: Rental income paid by the tenant must exceed the cost of repaying the borrowed money from the Public Works Loan Board (which is itself funded by the Government). The surplus is then an ancillary benefit which supports the Council's budget position and enables the Council to continue to provide services for local people.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Capital Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Council scheduled to cease 31 March 2028 under Local Government Reorganisation, creating governance uncertainty over two-year transition
findings.detail: West Devon Borough Council will cease to exist 31 March 2028 as part of LGR. Strategy documents continue to 2028/29 'for modelling and illustration purposes' only, but paper does not articulate how £24.96m debt, £14.9m investment properties, or £9.7m reserves will transition to successor authority or how long-term borrowing obligations will be discharged.
findings.matters: Organisational dissolution creates uncertainty about debt serviceability, asset ownership, and liabilities continuity affecting credit assessment and covenant compliance
findings.figures: Council dissolution 31 March 2028, current debt £24.96m, investment properties £14.9m, total reserves £9.7m
findings.quote: The current timetable for Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) is such that the District Council would cease on 31 st March 2028, for modelling and illustration purposes the 2028/29 financial year has continued to be shown.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Capital Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Council debt of £24.96m represents 242% of core spending power with unearmarked reserves at only 19.2% of net revenue spend
findings.detail: As at 31 January 2026, external borrowing is £25.9m. Total debt of £24.96m is 242% of core spending power (£10.31m). Unearmarked reserves of £1.9m represent only 19.2% of net revenue spend (£9.89m). Annual debt-servicing costs are £1.44m, consuming 14.6% of net revenue in 2026/27, leaving limited margin for revenue shortfalls.
findings.matters: High debt-to-income ratios combined with thin reserves indicate vulnerability to revenue shocks or income disruptions
findings.figures: £24.96m total debt, 242% of core spending power, unearmarked reserves £1.9m (19.2% of net revenue), debt-service costs £1.44m (14.6% of net revenue)
findings.quote: Appendix H to the Budget Proposals report for 2026/27 (Council 17th February 2026) sets out the following financial metrics: - Unearmarked Reserves as % of net revenue spend - £1,900,000/ £9,892,995 = 19.2% - Total debt as a % of core spending power - £24,955,700 / £10,314,000 = 242%

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Capital Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Okehampton Interchange Railway Station budget increased by £3.2m mid-project to £18.34m total
findings.detail: West Devon's £13.4m Levelling Up bid for railway station and transport hub has seen capital budget increased by £3.2m (total £18.34m). Cost revision made by Devon County Council in 2025 reflecting current market rates and adjustment of COVID-era estimates. Project expected completion May 2026, funded from S106 contributions received by Devon County Council.
findings.matters: Cost escalation on major infrastructure projects indicates inflation risk and project control issues affecting capital planning and borrowing requirements
findings.figures: £3.2m increase, total £18.34m (originally £13.4m Levelling Up funding), May 2026 completion
findings.quote: The capital budget for the railway station has been increased by £3.2million (total £18.34m), which is funded from S106 contributions received by DCC. The station's cost estimate was revised by DCC in 2025 to reflect current market rates and to reflect the fact that the original estimates were produced during the COVID pandemic.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Capital Strategy, 2026/27 Treasury Management Strategy and 2026/27 Investment Strategy
findings.headline: Investment income budget increased to £1.1 million for 2026/27
findings.detail: Treasury and investment income is budgeted at £1.1 million, up from £950,000 in 2025/26 — a 15.8% increase. This represents material revenue contribution to council finances from cash and investment management.
findings.matters: Investment income contributes to budget sustainability; an upward trend supports debt service capacity and financial resilience, but relies on continued interest rate environment and asset valuations
findings.figures: £1.1 million budgeted for 2026/27; £950,000 in 2025/26
findings.quote: The budget for investment income has increased for 2026/27 and has been set at £1.1m (this was £950,000 in 2025/26).

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Capital Strategy, 2026/27 Treasury Management Strategy and 2026/27 Investment Strategy
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement of £23.6 million for 2026/27, including four investment properties alongside operational schemes
findings.detail: The Council's underlying need to borrow is projected at £23.6 million for 2026/27. Borrowing will fund operational capital schemes (waste fleet, leisure facilities, Kilworthy Park development) and four commercial investment properties. The composition mixes asset replacement with commercial investment.
findings.matters: A lender needs the scale and composition of planned borrowing to assess debt service demands and understand whether the council is deploying capital for service delivery or commercial revenue generation
findings.figures: £23.6 million Capital Financing Requirement for 2026/27
findings.quote: the Capital Financing Requirement, the measure of the Council's underlying need to borrow for the capital programme, has been projected to be £23.6 million for 2026/27. This includes borrowing for the waste fleet, leisure, Kilworthy Park and four investment properties.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C – Investment Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: CCLA Property Fund reclassified to FVPL accounting treatment, held under expiring government accounting override
findings.detail: The council holds £500,000 in the CCLA Local Authorities Property Fund. In the year ended 31 March 2025, the council reclassified this investment from Fair Value through Other Comprehensive Income (FVOCI) to Fair Value through Profit and Loss (FVPL). Under normal FVPL accounting, unrealised gains and losses would impact the revenue account; however, the council relies on a government Pooled Investment Fund override that requires these gains/losses to be held on the balance sheet instead. This override expires 31 March 2029.
findings.matters: The £500k investment's accounting treatment depends on a time-limited government relief expiring in 2029; if not renewed, it could affect the council's reported financial position and revenue account volatility
findings.figures: £500,000 CCLA investment; intended holding period up to 7 years; accounting override expires 31 March 2029; CCLA is the only non-specified investment held (maximum £4 million permitted for non-specified investments)
findings.quote: the long-term investment with the CCLA Property Fund previously classified at Fair Value through Other Comprehensive Income (FVOCI) was reclassified to Fair Value through Profit and Loss (FVPL).

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Treasury Management 2026/27
findings.headline: The council will not take new external borrowing over the next three years, relying wholly on existing debt to fund the Capital Financing Requirement.
findings.detail: West Devon explicitly states it expects no new external loans through 2028/29. Instead, it will manage capital spending from the existing borrowing portfolio and drawing on reserves. This locks the council into a fixed debt structure and reduces flexibility to respond to new spending needs or borrowing rate opportunities.
findings.matters: Inflexibility on borrowing can be a weakness if unexpected spending emerges or if interest rate movements create refinancing pressure. Lenders want councils to have optionality.
findings.quote: The Council is not expecting to take any new external loans during the current and next two financial years as the current Capital Financing Requirement estimates will be fully financed by existing borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Treasury Management 2026/27
findings.headline: The £13.4m Okehampton railway station is expected to open in May 2026 with total cost now £18.34m, up £3.2m from original estimate.
findings.detail: West Devon is the accountable body for a Department for Transport funded Levelling Up project to build a new station and transport hub at Okehampton. The scheme cost has risen by £3.2m (18% increase) during development, funded from S106 contributions held by Devon County Council. The opening is imminent (May 2026) and the capital spend is now in the 2026/27 budget.
findings.matters: Large capital projects carry delivery risk. The cost increase and tight timeline suggest this may consume resources. Lenders monitor major one-off projects as they can strain cashflow and mask underlying spending pressures.
findings.figures: Original Levelling Up grant: £13.4m; cost increase from DCC re-estimate: £3.2m; total: £18.34m; expected completion: May 2026
findings.quote: The capital budget for the railway station has been increased by £3.2million (total £18.34m), which is funded from S106 contributions received by DCC. The station's cost estimate was revised by DCC in 2025 to reflect current market rates and to reflect the fact that the original estimates were produced during the COVID pandemic. It is expected that the station will be brought into service in May 2026.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Treasury Management 2026/27
findings.headline: Non-treasury investment borrowing stands at 227.94% of net budget—nearly £20m owed for four investment properties worth £14.9m.
findings.detail: West Devon has four investment properties (purchased 2018/19, valued at £14.905m as at March 2025) against which it has borrowed £19.8m for 2026/27. The borrowing-to-budget ratio of 227.94% is high and concentrated in property. The council notes it is using external advisors (Savills) but the exposure is material.
findings.matters: High exposure to property investment borrowing creates a concentration risk. If property values fall or rental income drops, the council faces a mismatch between debt and asset value. Lenders scrutinise this as a source of latent loss.
findings.figures: Investment properties fair value: £14,905,000; borrowing for investment activities: £19,838,000 (2026/27); ratio: 227.94% of net budget
findings.quote: Borrowing for Non-Treasury investments as a proportion of the Council's Net Budget 227.94%

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Treasury Management 2026/27
findings.headline: Fund balances are projected to decline steeply, from £11.7m to £7.9m over three years.
findings.detail: West Devon's general fund reserves are eroding at roughly £1m per year through the medium term. The decline is driven by capital spending (the railway station) and use of reserves to reduce borrowing. By 2028/29, reserves will have fallen by 33% from their 2025/26 level, shrinking the council's financial buffer.
findings.matters: Declining reserves reduce a council's ability to absorb one-off costs, fund spending gaps, or manage unexpected income loss. For lenders, this signals deteriorating financial resilience.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Treasury Management 2026/27
findings.headline: The council is overborrowed in the short term, though the gap narrows to £102k by 2027/28.
findings.detail: West Devon's gross debt exceeds its Capital Financing Requirement by £1,373,000 in 2026/27. The paper acknowledges this position directly and projects it will shrink to just £102k by 2027/28 as capital spending winds down after the Okehampton station completion. This is a short-term cash management issue rather than structural insolvency, but it signals tight cashflow.
findings.matters: Overborrowing limits the council's financial flexibility and reduces its ability to respond to unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls. Lenders monitor this as a sign of stretched finances.
findings.figures: External Debt 2026/27: £25,355,000; CFR (minus leases): £23,583,000; shortfall: £1,373,000
findings.quote: Although the Council is overborrowed in the short term, this becomes minimal in 2027/28 at only £102k difference.

findings.paper_title: Appendix H – Sensitivity analysis and risk assessment
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creates strategic uncertainty: West Devon District ceases 31st March 2028
findings.detail: West Devon is subject to planned Local Government Reorganisation, with the District Council scheduled to cease on 31st March 2028 (20 months from the budget date). This creates fundamental uncertainty about the council's future structure, management continuity, responsibility for existing debt, and ability to execute medium-term strategy beyond the reorganisation date.
findings.matters: Lenders assess council viability and creditworthiness; reorganisation creates material uncertainty about the post-2028 entity's structure, management, and responsibility for outstanding borrowing
findings.figures: West Devon District Council cease date 31st March 2028
findings.quote: Although the current timetable for Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) is such that the District Council would cease on 31st March 2028, for modelling and illustration purposes the 2028/29 financial year has continued to be shown.

findings.paper_title: Appendix H – Sensitivity analysis and risk assessment
findings.headline: CIPFA benchmarking identifies unearmarked reserves as higher risk compared to nearest neighbours and peer districts
findings.detail: Although unearmarked reserves of £1.9m (19.2% of net revenue spend) meet the recommended minimum of £1.25m, CIPFA's Financial Resilience Index flags them as higher risk when compared to nearest neighbours and non-metropolitan districts. Total reserves are predicted to decrease to £9.719m by 2026-27.
findings.matters: Reserves below peer-group averages indicate weaker shock-absorption capacity; lower financial cushion means less ability to handle unexpected revenue pressures or emergencies
findings.figures: Unearmarked reserves £1.9m (19.2% of net revenue spend), minimum recommended £1.25m, total reserves £9.72m (98% of net revenue budget)
findings.quote: Unallocated Reserves are higher risk when benchmarked against nearest neighbours and non metropolitan Districts.

findings.paper_title: Appendix H – Sensitivity analysis and risk assessment
findings.headline: Total borrowing of £24.96m represents 242% of core spending power, limiting future borrowing headroom
findings.detail: West Devon's total debt is £24,955,700 against core spending power of £10,314,000. Annual debt servicing (principal and interest) totals £1,441,500, representing 14% of core spending power. The council confirms all borrowing is fixed-rate and long-term, reducing interest rate risk, but the absolute leverage is substantial.
findings.matters: High debt-to-spending-power ratios limit future borrowing capacity and indicate heavy capital investment relative to revenue base; constrains financial flexibility for unexpected needs
findings.figures: Total debt £24.96m, core spending power £10.31m (242% ratio), debt servicing £1.44m annually (14% of core spending power)
findings.quote: Total debt as a % of core spending power - £24,955,700 / £10,314,000 = 242%

findings.paper_title: Appendix H – Sensitivity analysis and risk assessment
findings.headline: Council tax collection rate declining from 98.69% (2024-25 actual) to 97.75% (2026-27 assumed)
findings.detail: The council achieved 98.69% collection in 2024-25, ranking 13th nationally among billing authorities. The budget deliberately assumes 97.75% for 2026-27 onwards — a decline of 94 basis points. A 1% shortfall in collection would result in £62,770 less annual income.
findings.matters: Declining collection rates indicate weakening council tax cash flow or increasing householder financial stress; affects annual cash position and shows increasing collection risk
findings.figures: 2024-25 actual 98.69%, 2026-27 assumed 97.75% (decline of 94 basis points), 1% variation = £62,770
findings.quote: with a council tax collection rate of 97.75% (98.69% was achieved in 2024/25, which placed the Council 13th nationally out of 296 Councils who are Billing Authorities)

findings.paper_title: Appendix H – Sensitivity analysis and risk assessment
findings.headline: New Homes Bonus scheme providing £0.2m ceased at end of 2025-26 with no replacement identified
findings.detail: The New Homes Bonus scheme ended 31st March 2026, removing a permanent £0.2m annual funding source. The document does not identify a replacement for this structural funding loss, which the council must address through service reductions, income generation, or savings in future budgets.
findings.matters: Permanent funding losses reduce financial flexibility and force difficult choices between service cuts and finding alternative income; signals future budget pressure
findings.figures: £0.2m annual funding loss
findings.quote: The New Homes Bonus Scheme ceased at the end of 2025/26 (representing a loss of funding of £0.2m).

findings.paper_title: Appendix H – Sensitivity analysis and risk assessment
findings.headline: Fees and charges income flagged as higher risk due to small council budget and high proportion of revenue base
findings.detail: The council budgets £6m from fees, charges, recycling and investments. A 5% reduction would cost £300k. CIPFA's Financial Resilience Index specifically identifies this income stream as higher risk relative to peer councils because West Devon's smaller net budget means fees represent a larger proportion of total income.
findings.matters: Small councils with high proportion of discretionary income face greater vulnerability if demand or pricing assumptions shift; indicates weaker financial resilience
findings.figures: £6m in fees and charges income, 5% reduction = £300k
findings.quote: Fees and charges are also higher risk due to the smaller net budget of the Council and the higher proportion of the budget which fees and charges account for.

findings.paper_title: Appendix H – Sensitivity analysis and risk assessment
findings.headline: Investment property rental income of £1.2m annually flagged as higher financial risk in CIPFA index
findings.detail: The council holds investment properties generating £1.2m in rental income. CIPFA's Financial Resilience Index identifies interest payable on borrowings as higher risk specifically due to these holdings. A 10% loss in property rental income would cost £120k; a 1% variation in interest rates on investment income has a £200k impact.
findings.matters: Investment property income is volatile and discretionary; lenders assess income stability and the council's exposure to property market downturns or interest rate changes while servicing significant debt
findings.figures: £1.2m rental income, 10% loss = £120k, 1% interest rate variation = £200k
findings.quote: A 10% loss on investment property rental income equates to £120,000 (total rental income of £1.2m).

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Budget pressures and savings
findings.headline: Salary vacancy savings target doubled to £160,000 on a total payroll of £6.5 million
findings.detail: West Devon is increasing its salary vacancy savings from £80,000 in 2025/26 to £160,000 in 2026/27. On a payroll base of £6.5 million, this represents a 2.5% vacancy rate assumption, which is historically difficult for councils to achieve consistently and creates delivery risk.
findings.matters: Reliance on ambitious and uncertain vacancy savings to achieve budget balance means the council's financial plan is dependent on achieving consistently high vacancy rates, which are notoriously volatile
findings.figures: Vacancy saving target £80,000 (2025/26); proposed £160,000 (2026/27); total payroll £6.5m for 2025/26
findings.quote: Vacancy saving target on salaries - current budgeted target of £80,000 in 25-26. Projected to increase this to £160,000 for 26/27 (total pay of £6.5m for 25/26)

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Budget pressures and savings
findings.headline: Identified savings are heavily front-loaded in 2025/26 with minimal ongoing savings as cost pressures continue
findings.detail: Total identified savings of £1,798,000 are achieved in 2025/26, but this drops sharply to only £557,500 in 2026/27 and zero in 2027/28 onwards. Meanwhile, identified budget pressures remain at £1,652,000 in 2026/27 and £1,175,000 from 2027/28 onwards. This pattern of front-loaded savings with continuing structural pressures leaves the council increasingly exposed.
findings.matters: Savings concentrated in the current year with no sustained efficiencies in future years indicate the council has exhausted one-off opportunities and faces growing structural deficits
findings.quote: TOTAL SAVINGS AND INCOME GENERATION 1,798,000 557,500 0 0

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Budget pressures and savings
findings.headline: Council explicitly pre-funds an acknowledged 2027/28 budget gap using a one-off reserve contribution
findings.detail: The budget proposals show a £200,000 contribution into a financial sustainability reserve to address a known budget gap, with that amount drawn back down in 2027/28. This indicates West Devon recognizes it faces a structural budget shortfall in 2027/28 but is attempting to paper over it with a temporary reserve drawdown rather than implementing sustained structural solutions.
findings.matters: Pre-funding a known budget gap with one-off reserve use signals the council cannot balance its budget from ongoing operations and leaves no buffer for further pressures
findings.figures: £200,000 contributed to reserve in 2026/27; same amount drawn down in 2027/28
findings.quote: Contribution into a financial sustainability reserve to assist meeting the budget gap in 27/280 200,000

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Budget pressures and savings
findings.headline: Waste service costs of £400,000 per year from 2026/27 onwards funded by a temporary DEFRA grant with a significant funding cliff
findings.detail: West Devon faces permanent additional waste and recycling costs of £400,000 annually from 2026/27 onwards. These costs are being funded in 2026/27 via a DEFRA Extended Producer Responsibility grant of £1,103,500, with £1.078 million built into the permanent budget. However, this grant drops to just £25,500 in 2027/28 and disappears entirely thereafter, creating a structural funding gap of approximately £375,000 per year.
findings.matters: Building permanent service costs into base budget using temporary grant funding creates an unsustainable position when the grant expires, requiring either service cuts, reserve depletion, or future council tax increases
findings.figures: Additional waste costs £400,000 per year (2026/27 onwards); EPR grant £1,103,500 (2026/27), £25,500 (2027/28), then £0; £1.078m of grant built into base budget
findings.quote: Recommend to build all of this Government grant funding (£1.078m in total) into the 26/27 base budget to fund waste expenditure from 26/27 onwards

findings.paper_title: Appendix G – Summary of the Budget Book for 2026/27
findings.headline: Loss of New Homes Bonus and Business Rates Pooling Gain as government funding rebalances
findings.detail: West Devon receives no New Homes Bonus or Business Rates Pooling Gain in 26/27 (down from £216,009 and £185,000 respectively in 25/26), a combined loss of £401,009. This is partially offset by a large increase in Revenue Support Grant (£112,477 → £2,076,557), but the composition of funding is shifting materially.
findings.matters: Reliance on volatile government grants is a credit risk; losing performance-based funding (NHB, pooling gains) in favour of flat RSG is a structural change that may not be reversible if political priorities shift.
findings.figures: New Homes Bonus: £216,009 → £0; Business Rates Pooling Gain: £185,000 → £0; Revenue Support Grant: £112,477 → £2,076,557
findings.quote: New Homes Bonus 216,009 0 / Business Rates Pooling Gain 185,000 0 / Revenue Support Grant 112,477 2,076,557

findings.paper_title: Appendix G – Summary of the Budget Book for 2026/27
findings.headline: Inflation budget of £275,000 remains unallocated, with workings still ongoing
findings.detail: The budget sets aside £275,000 explicitly for inflation on a single line, with a note stating 'the detailed workings for exact distribution across services are ongoing'. This indicates the budget has not been fully finalized and the council has not yet identified which services will absorb inflation pressures.
findings.matters: An incomplete budget allocation late in the financial planning cycle suggests either tight timelines or uncertainty about inflation impacts. Services may face real-terms cuts if allocated inflation is insufficient.
findings.figures: £275,000 inflation allocation
findings.quote: Inflation is showing on one line as the detailed workings for exact distribution across services are ongoing.

findings.paper_title: Appendix G – Summary of the Budget Book for 2026/27
findings.headline: Council draws £755,850 from earmarked reserves to balance the 2026/27 budget
findings.detail: The budget relies on a net draw of £755,850 from earmarked reserves to fund operations in 2026/27. This follows a larger drawdown of £1,320,400 in 2025/26. Reliance on reserve depletion to cover ongoing revenue signals the underlying budget is structurally tight.
findings.matters: Reserves are finite and one-off. Drawing them down year-on-year to close a structural gap is unsustainable and signals the council cannot fund current operations from ongoing revenue alone.
findings.quote: Contributions (to)/from Earmarked Reserves (1,320,400) (755,850)

findings.paper_title: Appendix G – Summary of the Budget Book for 2026/27
findings.headline: Waste and Cleansing cost jumps 13.5%, the largest single budget adjustment in the council
findings.detail: The Waste Collection, Recycling and Cleansing service grows from £3,440,200 to £3,906,000, a £465,800 increase. This is the single largest budget proposal adjustment across all three service groups. Waste services often carry latent inflation and operational pressures; a 13.5% year-on-year jump signals either service expansion, acute cost inflation in this area, or efficiency headwinds.
findings.matters: Waste and environmental services typically have inelastic demand and volatile input costs; sustained pressure here can compress reserves quickly and signal underlying operational stress.
findings.quote: W1990 Waste Collection, Recyling & Cleansing Sarah Moody 3,440,200 465,800 0 3,906,000

findings.paper_title: Appendix C – Transfers to/from Reserves
findings.headline: Investment property management reserve increased to 15% of investment income
findings.detail: The council is increasing its management, maintenance and risk reserve for investment properties to 15% of annual investment income (£165,000 per annum). This is a step-up in the contribution rate.
findings.matters: An increase in the proportion of investment income reserved for management and risk suggests either a growing investment portfolio or anticipated higher maintenance or risk costs, signalling complexity in the council's investment strategy.
findings.figures: 15% rate; £165,000 per annum for 25/26
findings.quote: Management, Maintenance and Risk Management Reserve for Investment properties (increases contribution to 15% of investment income for 25/26, i.e. £165,000 per annum)

findings.paper_title: Appendix C – Transfers to/from Reserves
findings.headline: Housing service restructuring through post reductions
findings.detail: Housing services are delivering efficiency savings by eliminating a post and reducing external grant income. The specific amount is not itemised separately but is part of the £216,009 noted.
findings.matters: Service restructuring, particularly through staff reductions, can indicate capacity constraints and may affect service delivery or corporate capability; repeated rounds of this indicate a council under financial pressure.
findings.figures: Amount not separately stated; part of housing-related withdrawals
findings.quote: Housing service efficiency savings - savings of a post and external grant income

findings.paper_title: Appendix C – Transfers to/from Reserves
findings.headline: New Homes Bonus funding reduction of £216,009 in 2025/26
findings.detail: The council explicitly notes that NHB funding of £216,009 is being withdrawn in 2025/26. This is a direct loss of central government grant income with no apparent replacement identified in this reserve schedule.
findings.matters: Government grant reductions are a permanent loss to the council's funding base; they cannot be absorbed from reserves indefinitely and typically force service reductions or efficiency savings.
findings.figures: £216,009 withdrawal; total planned contributions in 25/26 of £1,320,400 net of this reduction
findings.quote: The amount of £1,104,391 equates to contributions to reserves of £1,320,400 in 25/26, less NHB funding in 25/26 of £216,009.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C – Transfers to/from Reserves
findings.headline: Council building a reserve to cover an anticipated budget gap in 2027/28
findings.detail: West Devon is creating a new financial sustainability reserve with a £200,000 contribution in 2026/27 explicitly stated as 'to assist meeting the budget gap in 27/28'. This indicates the council has already identified a funding shortfall two years out and is putting aside money to absorb it.
findings.matters: Forward budget gaps are a key lending risk; the council is being proactive but the very fact they are pre-funding suggests the gap is material and their operating revenue cannot cover it.
findings.figures: £200,000 in 2026/27; net reserve contributions declining from £1,104,391 (25/26) to £755,850 (26/27)
findings.quote: Contribution into a financial sustainability reserve to assist meeting the budget gap in 27/28

findings.paper_title: Draft Revenue and Capital Budget Proposals 2026/27
findings.headline: External auditor assessment: Green rating across financial sustainability, governance and efficiency; no significant weaknesses
findings.detail: Bishop Fleming's Auditor's Annual Report for 2024-25 (considered 2 December 2025) assigned the council a 'Green rating' for all three areas: financial sustainability, governance, and the 3 Es (economy, efficiency and effectiveness). The auditor did not identify any significant weaknesses and made no recommendations. This provides independent validation of current position, though does not address the forward budget gaps.
findings.matters: Clean audit opinion supports the council's governance and financial control framework, but the gap between current audit assessment and emerging 2027-28 deficits means audit findings may not have captured forward-looking stress.
findings.figures: Green rating across three assessment areas
findings.quote: The Council was scored as a 'Green rating' for all three areas of financial sustainability, governance, and the 3 E's (economy, efficiency and effectiveness). Their report stated that they did not identify any significant weaknesses and did not make any recommendations.

findings.paper_title: Draft Revenue and Capital Budget Proposals 2026/27
findings.headline: Positive: Pension fund deficit improved and employer contribution rate reduced by approximately £95,000 per annum
findings.detail: The triennial revaluation of the Devon Pension Fund (as at 31 March 2025) shows West Devon's proportion at 92.8% funding level, up from 90% in 2022, representing a £0.66m improvement in the deficit. The council's employer contribution rate can be reduced from 17.8% to 16.7% for the three years to March 2029, yielding approximately £95,000 annual savings.
findings.matters: Pension cost reductions provide rare good news and free up budget headroom during a period of structural funding pressure, though the deficit remains material at £2.64m.
findings.figures: Funding level improved from 90% (2022) to 92.8% (2025); deficit £2.64m; contribution rate reduction 17.8% to 16.7%; annual saving £95,000
findings.quote: The actuary has advised that the primary rate contributions of the Council can be reduced from 17.8% to 16.7% for the three years to 31 March 2029. This is a reduction of approximately £95,000 per annum.

findings.paper_title: Draft Revenue and Capital Budget Proposals 2026/27
findings.headline: Council restructuring due to local government reorganisation (unitary merger) takes effect 31 March 2028
findings.detail: West Devon is scheduled to cease as a district council on 31 March 2028 as part of unitary local government reorganisation. This creates a planning horizon constraint: the council must balance budgets and manage reserves across a three-year planning window that ends with organisational dissolution. The paper continues to model 2028/29 'for illustration purposes' but the restructuring adds execution risk.
findings.matters: An impending organisational restructuring constrains management discretion, complicates workforce planning and asset management, and may complicate creditor relationships during the transition period.
findings.figures: Unitary merger effective 31 March 2028
findings.quote: Although the current timetable for Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) is such that the District Council would cease on 31st March 2028, for modelling and illustration purposes the 2028/29 financial year has continued to be shown.

findings.paper_title: Draft Revenue and Capital Budget Proposals 2026/27
findings.headline: Treasury investment income stretched to £1.1m amid falling interest rates, down from £1.3m achieved in 2025/26
findings.detail: The council is setting a stretched treasury management income target of £1.1m for 2026/27, despite predicting at least £1.3m for 2025/26. This reduction reflects the Bank of England rate cuts from 3.75% in December 2025 to an expected 3.5% by summer 2026, reducing the yield on the council's cash holdings.
findings.matters: Declining interest income from lower rates removes an income buffer the council has relied on and forces further structural adjustments or reliance on reserves.
findings.figures: Treasury income target 2026/27: £1.1m; predicted 2025/26: £1.3m; base rate December 2025: 3.75%; predicted summer 2026: 3.5%
findings.quote: At least £1.3m of income is predicted for 2025/26 and this would provide a stretched income target for 26/27. In December 2025 the bank base rate was cut to 3.75%. Rates are predicted to drop to 3.5% during Summer 2026.

findings.paper_title: Draft Revenue and Capital Budget Proposals 2026/27
findings.headline: Waste and recycling service cost pressure of £400,000 is largest identified cost pressure
findings.detail: The council has built in £400,000 for waste, recycling and cleansing cost pressures in 2026/27. This is among the largest single cost drivers identified in the budget and reflects either service volume growth or price inflation. The council is partially offsetting this via Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) DEFRA grant, but the underlying service cost is material.
findings.matters: A significant and growing cost pressure in a statutory service indicates either efficiency challenges or demand-driven costs that may persist and grow, affecting future budget sustainability.
findings.figures: Waste cost pressure £400,000; EPR DEFRA grant offsetting approximately £803,500
findings.quote: Additional costs associated with the waste, recycling and cleansing service have been estimated at £400,000.

findings.paper_title: Draft Revenue and Capital Budget Proposals 2026/27
findings.headline: Material grant income losses: New Homes Bonus ends (£0.2m) and UKSPF funding ceases, requiring £200,000 continued investment
findings.detail: The New Homes Bonus scheme ceased entirely at end of 2025/26, removing £0.2m annual income. Separately, UKSPF (UK Shared Prosperity Fund) ends after 2025/26, requiring the council to budget £200,000 to continue business support that was previously grant-funded. These are structural income losses requiring either service cuts or substitute funding.
findings.matters: Loss of non-council-tax income streams reduces the council's financial resilience and requires compensating savings elsewhere or reliance on discretionary reserves.
findings.figures: New Homes Bonus loss £0.2m; UKSPF continuation cost £200,000
findings.quote: The New Homes Bonus Scheme ceased at the end of 2025/26 (representing a loss of funding of £0.2m). Supporting Economic Development activities (£200,000) – A cost pressure of £200,000 has been built into the budget process for 2026/27 for a continuation of business support previously provided through the UKSPF Fund

findings.paper_title: Draft Revenue and Capital Budget Proposals 2026/27
findings.headline: Reserve position eroding from 150% of annual budget to 98%, constraining future flexibility
findings.detail: Reserves are projected to fall from 150% of net revenue budget in 2024 to 98% by 2027. The council currently holds £1.82m in unearmarked reserves (set minimum £1.25m) and is proposing to transfer £200,000 into a Financial Sustainability reserve to help bridge the 2027/28 gap. This trajectory suggests the council's financial buffer is tightening rapidly as it approaches the 2028 local government reorganisation deadline.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion limits a council's ability to absorb unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls and may signal increased financial stress if the trajectory continues.
findings.figures: Reserves 150% (2024) to 98% (2027); unearmarked reserves £1.82m; minimum operating level £1.25m; transfer to Financial Sustainability reserve £200,000
findings.quote: It can be seen by the table above that the percentage of reserves as a proportion of the Net Revenue Budget is reducing from 150% in 2024 to 98% in 2027.

findings.paper_title: Draft Revenue and Capital Budget Proposals 2026/27
findings.headline: Budget gaps of £546,540 in 2027/28 and £1.153m in 2028/29 require further action
findings.detail: The council achieves a balanced budget for 2026/27 but is forecasting substantial deficits in the following two years. The 2027/28 gap is described as 'significantly higher than normal at this point in the financial planning cycle' due to government announcements in the Finance Settlement. The council acknowledges it may need to use reserves to bridge these gaps but has not yet identified where these savings will come from.
findings.matters: Escalating budget gaps in the near term indicate structural budget stress that will require either service reductions, council tax rises, or reserve drawdown—all of which affect creditworthiness and financial flexibility.
findings.quote: The Council is currently forecasting a £546,540 budget gap by the following year, 2027/28 and a further budget gap of £1,153,407 in the 2028/29 financial year.

findings.paper_title: Draft Revenue and Capital Budget Proposals 2026/27
findings.headline: Government funding cut by 7.5% over three years hits rural council disproportionately
findings.detail: The Fair Funding Review has reduced West Devon's baseline funding level from £3.696m to £3.420m by 2028/29. The council has been hit particularly hard by the removal of the remoteness factor from the funding formula and reduction in visitor/commuter population weighting, both of which disadvantage sparsely populated areas with large travel distances. Rural councils in the same period see only 1% spending power increase versus 21% for urban authorities.
findings.matters: A lender assessing risk must understand whether the council can maintain service delivery and debt servicing as its government funding base contracts sharply in real terms.
findings.figures: 7.5% reduction (£0.276m); funding from £3.696m to £3.420m; rural vs urban spending power increase 1% vs 21%
findings.quote: This is a reduction of £0.276m in the three year settlement (a 7.5% reduction). As a sparsely populated area with large travel distances, taking away the remoteness factor has impacted on West Devon quite heavily as it disadvantages more rural and remote Councils.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Modelling of the Budget Position
findings.headline: Business rates income is projected to decline significantly after 2025/26, offsetting some council tax gains
findings.detail: Localised business rates drop from £2,333,401 in 2025/26 to £1,563,363 in 2026/27 (a 33% fall). While the model assumes business rates growth returns from 2026/27 onwards (£189,595 growing to £250,000), the baseline remains substantially below the opening position.
findings.matters: Business rates volatility signals economic exposure. A major drop followed by modest recovery assumptions could underestimate risk if local economic conditions weaken.
findings.quote: Localised Business Rates (estimate of business rates resources received in the year) 2,333,401 1,563,363 1,599,224 1,631,489

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Modelling of the Budget Position
findings.headline: Revenue Support Grant structure changes significantly from April 2026 under the new funding system
findings.detail: The council's Revenue Support Grant shifts from £112,477 in 2025/26 under the old system to £2,076,557 in 2026/27 under the new system announced for April 2026. The new system grant then declines to £1,938,902 in 2027/28 and £1,788,893 in 2028/29.
findings.matters: A major structural change in a council's core funding (an 18-fold increase followed by progressive decline) creates uncertainty. Lenders need confidence this transition is sustainable and the projections realistic.
findings.quote: Revenue Support Grant (previous funding system) 112,477 0 0 0; Revenue Support Grant (new funding system from April 2026) n/a 2,076,557 1,938,902 1,788,893

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Modelling of the Budget Position
findings.headline: A £1.7m cumulative budget gap emerges from 2027/28, with no identified savings to close it
findings.detail: The budget model projects a £546,540 deficit in 2027/28 and £1,153,407 in 2028/29. The cumulative gap by 2028/29 reaches £1,699,947. Critically, the savings plan identified in the budget (£1,798,000 in 2025/26, £557,500 in 2026/27) ends entirely by 2027/28, while budget pressures of £1,175,000 per year persist.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council has a credible plan to close an emerging deficit. The model shows the savings plan is front-loaded and exhausted before the gap appears, leaving no identified solution.
findings.figures: Budget gap 2027/28: £546,540; 2028/29: £1,153,407; Cumulative gap: £1,699,947; Savings 2027/28 onwards: £0; Budget pressures 2027/28-2028/29: £1,175,000 each year
